CALIFORNIA COMPREHENSIVE COMPUTER DATA ACCESS AND FRAUD ACT — DEMAND LETTER INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE OF THIS LETTER
This letter is sent by Acme, Inc. to Jordan Lee concerning a computer, computer system, computer network, or data that Acme, Inc. owns, leases, or otherwise controls. Acme, Inc. identifies the computer, system, network, or data at issue as follows: Acme, Inc.'s internal customer database and CRM system

Based on information currently available to Acme, Inc., the following describes conduct that Acme, Inc. believes may involve access to that computer, system, network, or data: On March 3, 2026, the respondent appeared outside the petitioner’s home and yelled threats for several minutes before leaving.

This description reflects Acme, Inc.'s current understanding. It is not a judicial finding, and nothing in this letter states that a court has determined that any violation occurred. Acme, Inc. is sending this letter to describe its concerns and to request specific actions in response, by no later than September 15, 2026.

STATUTORY PROHIBITED ACTS UNDER PENAL CODE SECTION 502(C)
California Penal Code section 502(c) lists specific acts that, when committed knowingly, are a public offense. Among the acts listed: knowingly accessing and, without permission, altering, damaging, deleting, destroying, or otherwise using data, a computer, a computer system, or a computer network in order to devise or execute a scheme to defraud, deceive, or extort, or to wrongfully control or obtain money, property, or data; knowingly accessing and, without permission, taking, copying, or making use of data from a computer, computer system, or computer network, or taking or copying supporting documentation; and knowingly and without permission using or causing to be used computer services. Subdivision (c) lists additional prohibited acts beyond these three, including adding or altering data, disrupting computer services, providing a means of unauthorized access, introducing a computer contaminant, and provisions specific to government and public-safety-infrastructure computer systems.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(c) Except as provided in subdivision (h), any person who commits any of the following acts is guilty of a public offense: (1) Knowingly accesses and without permission alters, damages, deletes, destroys, or otherwise uses any data, computer, computer system, or computer network in order to either (A) devise or execute any scheme or artifice to defraud, deceive, or extort, or (B) wrongfully control or obtain money, property, or data. (2) Knowingly accesses and without permission takes, copies, or makes use of any data from a computer, computer system, or computer network, or takes or copies any supporting documentation, whether existing or residing internal or external to a computer, computer system, or computer network. (3) Knowingly and without permission uses or causes to be used computer services."
  — Cal. Penal Code § 502(c) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Comprehensive Computer Data Access and Fraud Act, prohibited acts (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=502.)
  Known gap: Cal. Penal Code § 502(c) lists fourteen numbered prohibited acts, (1) through (14); this clause quotes only the introductory clause and paragraphs (1) through (3), the acts most commonly at issue in a private unauthorized-access dispute. It does not quote paragraphs (4) through (14), the felony/misdemeanor/infraction punishment schedule in subdivision (d), the forfeiture provision in subdivision (g), or the lawful-employment exemption in subdivision (h) -- all of which affect how subdivision (c) applies and are not otherwise addressed by this document. This clause does not state that any specific access was or was not authorized, or that any specific conduct falls within one of these paragraphs.

CIVIL CAUSE OF ACTION FOR UNAUTHORIZED COMPUTER ACCESS
California law gives the owner or lessee of a computer, computer system, computer network, computer program, or data a private civil cause of action against a person who violates Penal Code section 502(c), where the owner or lessee suffers damage or loss by reason of that violation. This civil action is available in addition to any other civil remedy that may exist. A court may award compensatory damages and injunctive relief or other equitable relief; compensatory damages include any expenditure reasonably and necessarily incurred by the owner or lessee to verify whether a computer system, computer network, computer program, or data was or was not altered, damaged, or deleted by the access.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(e) (1) In addition to any other civil remedy available, the owner or lessee of the computer, computer system, computer network, computer program, or data who suffers damage or loss by reason of a violation of any of the provisions of subdivision (c) may bring a civil action against the violator for compensatory damages and injunctive relief or other equitable relief. Compensatory damages shall include any expenditure reasonably and necessarily incurred by the owner or lessee to verify that a computer system, computer network, computer program, or data was or was not altered, damaged, or deleted by the access."
  — Cal. Penal Code § 502(e)(1) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Comprehensive Computer Data Access and Fraud Act, private civil action (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=502.)
  Known gap: This is California statutory law, quoted from Cal. Penal Code § 502(e)(1), used as evidence of the existence and scope of the civil cause of action -- not a claim that any specific access violated subdivision (c), and not a claim that any specific person suffered damage or loss. Subdivision (e)(1) also imputes an unemancipated minor's conduct to a parent or legal guardian under Civil Code section 1714.1 for purposes of this civil action; that imputation provision is mentioned in the statute but not separately quoted or analyzed here.

ATTORNEY'S FEES AND PUNITIVE DAMAGES AVAILABLE UNDER SECTION 502
In an action brought under Penal Code section 502(e), the statute allows a court to award reasonable attorney's fees. Separately, where a violation of subdivision (c) was willful, and it is proved by clear and convincing evidence that the defendant acted with oppression, fraud, or malice as those terms are defined in Civil Code section 3294(c), the statute allows a court to additionally award punitive or exemplary damages.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(2) In any action brought pursuant to this subdivision the court may award reasonable attorney’s fees."
  — Cal. Penal Code § 502(e)(2) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Comprehensive Computer Data Access and Fraud Act, attorney's fees (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=502.)
  "(4) In any action brought pursuant to this subdivision for a willful violation of the provisions of subdivision (c), where it is proved by clear and convincing evidence that a defendant has been guilty of oppression, fraud, or malice as defined in subdivision (c) of Section 3294 of the Civil Code, the court may additionally award punitive or exemplary damages."
  — Cal. Penal Code § 502(e)(4) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Comprehensive Computer Data Access and Fraud Act, punitive damages (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=502.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes two paragraphs of the same statutory subdivision, Cal. Penal Code § 502(e) -- paragraph (2) (attorney's fees) and paragraph (4) (punitive damages) -- so these two citations are not independent of one another; both come from the same subdivision of the same section. Unlike some other fee-shifting statutes, subdivision (e)(2)'s text does not itself condition the fee award on which party prevails or on a bad-faith finding -- it states only that the court may award such fees in an action brought under the subdivision; this clause does not interpret how a court would exercise that discretion in practice. The punitive-damages standard in paragraph (4) incorporates by reference the definitions of oppression, fraud, and malice in Civil Code section 3294(c), which are not themselves quoted or independently verified here.

THREE-YEAR PERIOD TO BRING A CIVIL ACTION
A civil action under Penal Code section 502(e) may not be brought unless it is initiated within three years of the date of the act complained of, or the date of the discovery of the damage, whichever is later.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(5) No action may be brought pursuant to this subdivision unless it is initiated within three years of the date of the act complained of, or the date of the discovery of the damage, whichever is later."
  — Cal. Penal Code § 502(e)(5) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Comprehensive Computer Data Access and Fraud Act, limitations period (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=502.)
  Known gap: This is California statutory law, quoted from Cal. Penal Code § 502(e)(5) -- not a claim about when any specific act occurred or was discovered, and not a claim about whether any tolling doctrine might extend or suspend this three-year period in a specific case.

CASE LAW ADDRESSING THE SCOPE OF "WITHOUT PERMISSION"
Penal Code section 502 does not itself define the phrase "without permission," even though that phrase appears throughout the prohibited acts listed in subdivision (c); subdivision (b) separately defines fifteen other terms used in the section, and "without permission" is not among them. In Facebook, Inc. v. Power Ventures, Inc., the Ninth Circuit addressed how permission that was initially given can later be revoked for purposes of section 502: where a computer owner had impliedly authorized certain access and then expressly revoked that authorization -- there, through a cease-and-desist letter -- the court held that continued access after the party received that revocation was "without permission" within the meaning of section 502(c)(2).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "But when Facebook sent the cease and desist letter, Power, as it conceded, knew that it no longer had permission to access Facebook’s computers at all. Power, therefore, knowingly accessed and without permission took, copied, and made use of Facebook’s data. Accordingly, we affirm in part the district court’s holding, that Power violated section 502."
  — Facebook, Inc. v. Power Ventures, Inc., 844 F.3d 1058, 1069-70 (9th Cir. 2016) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/8443085/facebook-inc-v-power-ventures-inc/)
  Known gap: Facebook, Inc. v. Power Ventures, Inc., 844 F.3d 1058 (9th Cir. 2016), is a Ninth Circuit decision applying California law, not a decision of a California state court, so it is persuasive rather than binding authority on how a California state court would apply section 502. Its holding is tied to its facts -- an express, individualized cease-and-desist letter revoking previously implied permission -- and does not establish a general rule for every situation in which permission might be contested. The observation that subdivision (b)'s fifteen defined terms do not include "without permission" is this researcher's own count of the definitions listed in the fetched statutory text (the same text quoted in the prohibited-acts authority clause in this document); it is not a holding of any case, and no case specifically addressing the absence of that statutory definition was located.

HOW SECTION 502 DIFFERS FROM THE FEDERAL COMPUTER FRAUD AND ABUSE ACT
California's Penal Code section 502 and the federal Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA), 18 U.S.C. section 1030, are separate statutes, and conduct can potentially be examined under either or both. The Ninth Circuit has held that section 502 "is different" from the CFAA because, unlike the CFAA's requirement of unauthorized access, section 502 "does not require unauthorized access" and "merely requires knowing access" -- with the separate requirement, described in the prohibited-acts clause above, that the access be "without permission."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "This statute, we have held, is “different” than the CFAA. United States v. Christensen, 801 F.3d 970, 994 (2015). “[T]he California statute does not require unauthorized access. It merely requires knowing access."
  — Facebook, Inc. v. Power Ventures, Inc., 844 F.3d 1058, 1069 (9th Cir. 2016), quoting United States v. Christensen, 801 F.3d 970, 994 (9th Cir. 2015) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/8443085/facebook-inc-v-power-ventures-inc/)
  Known gap: This quote comes from the same case used in the preceding authority clause on the scope of "without permission" -- Facebook, Inc. v. Power Ventures, Inc., 844 F.3d 1058 (9th Cir. 2016) -- so these two clauses are not independent sources of case law from each other, even though each addresses a different point. The Ninth Circuit was itself quoting its own earlier decision, United States v. Christensen, 801 F.3d 970, 994 (9th Cir. 2015), which is not independently fetched or verified here. Like the previous clause, this is a federal court of appeals interpretation of California law, not a decision of a California state court. This clause addresses only the specific "knowing access" versus "unauthorized access" distinction the court identified; it does not compare every element of the two statutes, and it does not address the CFAA's own jurisdictional requirements, damage thresholds, or remedies, none of which were independently verified for this document.

REQUESTED ACTIONS, RESERVATION OF RIGHTS, AND SIGNATURE
Acme, Inc. requests that, by September 15, 2026, Jordan Lee: (1) stop any further access to, or use of, the computer, computer system, computer network, or data described above unless and until separately authorized; (2) preserve, without alteration or deletion, all records and communications related to the access described above; and (3) confirm the above in writing. Acme, Inc. requests a written response by that date.

Nothing in this letter is a complete statement of the facts, claims, or legal theories available to Acme, Inc. Nothing in this letter waives or limits any right or remedy Acme, Inc. may have, all of which are expressly reserved, whether or not specifically mentioned above.

Acme, Inc.
By: _______________
Date: _______________
